record.paper_title: Open Questions about Time and Self-reference in Living Systems
record.original_question: How can an evolutionary model with multiple possible trajectories be calibrated and validated when there may be many fewer datasets than possible model outcomes, and when unobserved outcomes may either be possible-but-unrealized consequences of a structurally correct model or impossible artifacts of a structurally incorrect model?

evidence.quote:
For example, to use most models of real systems for prediction, they must
be calibrated. How do we calibrate an evolutionary model with multiple possible trajectories when we
may have many fewer data sets than the model has possible outcomes? If we calibrate so that the
model produces only observed outcomes, then if the model is structurally correct we will have seriously
mis-calibrated it, so that the model cannot predict outcomes that could have happened but did not; on
the other hand, perhaps the model is structurally incorrect, and those unobserved outcomes could not
in fact have happened. We have no way of knowing which of these possibilities is the case. This is a
problem that already arises in dynamical models with bifurcating trajectories [132] and at present there
is no known method for resolving it.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a parametric stochastic dynamical model M(θ) of an evolutionary process whose state space and dynamics admit multiple possible trajectories from a given initial condition (for instance, a model with bifurcating trajectories or branching stochastic dynamics). For a parameter θ in some admissible set Θ, let O(θ) denote the (possibly very large or infinite) set of qualitatively distinct outcomes that the model can produce with positive probability, and let p_θ be the induced probability distribution on O(θ). Suppose we are given an empirical dataset D = {d_1, …, d_N} consisting of observed outcomes from N independent realizations of the real system, where N ≪ |O(θ)| for all θ ∈ Θ; in particular, many outcomes that the model assigns positive probability are not represented in D.

The calibration problem is to choose θ (and to validate the structural form of M) using D. Two failure modes are to be distinguished:

(a) Structural correctness with under-sampling: M(θ*) is structurally correct for some θ* ∈ Θ, and the unobserved outcomes in O(θ*) \ D are genuinely possible-but-unrealized consequences of the true process. Then any calibration procedure that adjusts θ so as to concentrate p_θ on the observed outcomes D (e.g. by maximum likelihood on D treated as exhaustive, or by penalizing outcomes outside D) will mis-calibrate the model and destroy its ability to predict outcomes that could have happened but did not.

(b) Structural incorrectness: no θ ∈ Θ makes M structurally correct, and the would-be outcomes in O(θ) \ D are artifacts of a misspecified model that could not in fact occur in the real system. Then calibration that preserves probability mass on O(θ) \ D will produce a model that predicts impossible outcomes.

Develop a principled methodology — for example, an estimator θ̂(D), a model-validation criterion, or an identifiability theorem — that, given only the dataset D and the model class {M(θ) : θ ∈ Θ}, can either:

(i) consistently calibrate θ while correctly preserving probability mass on possible-but-unobserved outcomes when the model class contains a structurally correct member, and simultaneously
(ii) detect structural incorrectness, i.e. distinguish case (a) from case (b),

or else prove a no-go result showing that, under stated assumptions on (Θ, M, the sampling distribution of D), no procedure depending only on D can asymptotically distinguish (a) from (b) as N grows with N ≪ |O(θ)|.
artifact.status_search_result: The problem of calibrating and validating stochastic/dynamical models with many more possible outcomes (e.g. bifurcating trajectories) than available datasets, and of distinguishing structural misspecification from under-sampling of a correct model, is a recognized open problem in the modeling of evolutionary and complex systems. No general-purpose method resolving this identifiability issue appears in the literature; related work on model validation under bifurcations and on simulation-based inference (ABC, neural posterior estimation) addresses parts of the issue but does not resolve the fundamental ambiguity between possible-but-unrealized and impossible outcomes.

status_evidence.title: Open Questions about Time and Self-reference in Living Systems
status_evidence.snippet: This is a problem that already arises in dynamical models with bifurcating trajectories and at present there is no known method for resolving it.
status_evidence.claim: The calibration/validation question for evolutionary models with many possible trajectories and few datasets is stated as currently unresolved.
